title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: Quinta close; GAR misnames tertia; Resp. 1
pass_a_gloss: If therefore God out of his supreme mercy and wisdom deferred the execution of that threat, and suspended it from another judgment future after the separation of soul from body, it must be confessed that Adam was not, as the law's threat carried, Dead. And so that threat concerning spiritual death placed in privation of justice is not to be understood [as I take the threat], which I judge to be a worse evil than eternal death itself. GAR. There is added also a third reason. If the law was threatening Adam with death situated in privation of justice, Adam, just as God had threatened, would have died, which is false; since he is not to be numbered among the damned. Likewise, since that death embraces the eternal, the bodily, and the spiritual, he who never felt the eternal, nor at once felt the temporal, how would he at once have incurred the spiritual, namely privation of justice? Reply 1. He who has died the death situated in privation of justice, if he perseveres in it unto the end, is to be numbered among the damned. But it was not so done to Adam, who by faith in the blessed seed was raised from that spiritual death into spiritual life, as it is with all the elect, whom dead in sins it please God to make alive in Christ, Eph. 2.
pass_b_english: If then God in supreme mercy and wisdom deferred executing that threat, hanging it on another judgment after soul and body part, we must grant Adam was not Dead as the law's threat required. So the threat of spiritual death as privation of righteousness is not to be read as I take that threat—which I judge a worse evil than eternal death itself.

Garissoles. A "third" reason is added. If the law threatened Adam with death as privation of righteousness, he would have died as God threatened—which is false, since he is not to be counted among the damned. And since that death covers eternal, bodily, and spiritual: he who never felt eternal death, nor at once felt temporal, how did he at once incur spiritual death—privation of righteousness? Reply 1. Whoever dies the death of privation of righteousness and stays in it to the end is counted among the damned. Not so Adam: by faith in the blessed seed he was raised from that spiritual death into spiritual life, as with all the elect whom God is pleased to make alive in Christ when dead in sins (Eph. 2).
source_text:
Si igitur Deus pro summa sua misericordia & sapientia comminationis illius executionem distulit, ac suspendit ex alio judicio post separationem animae a corpore futuro, fatendum est Adamum non fuisse, prout ferebat legis comminatio, Mortuum. Itaque comminationem illam de spirituali morte posita in privatione justitiae non esse intelligendam, quam ego arbitror ipsa morte aeterna deterius malum esse.

GAR. Additur & tertia ratio. Si lex Adamo mortem sitam in privatione justitiae comminabatur, Adamus, prout Deus comminatus erat, mortuus fuerit, quod falsum; cum inter damnatos non sit computandus. Item, cum mors illa aeternam, corporalem, & spiritualem complectatur, qui nunquam sensit aeternam, nec statim sensit temporalem, quomodo spiritualem, nempe privationem justitiae, statim incurrisset? Respond. 1. Qui mortuus est morte sita in privatione justitiae, si in ea perseveret, usque ad finem, inter damnatos computandus est. At non ita factum Adamo, qui fide in semen benedictum ex illa morte spirituali in vitam spiritualem excitatus est, ut fit omnibus electis, quos mortuos in peccatis placet Deo vivificare in Christo, Ephes. 2.

lemmas.gloss: the threat is not to be understood [thus]

choices.choice: not Dead as threatened; GAR misnames quinta as tertia; elect raised
